title: A happy number is defined by repeatedly replacing a number with the sum of the squares of its digits; if this process reaches 1 the number is happy, otherwise it loops endlessly. Determine whether a given number is happy. (LeetCode: Happy Number)
shortTitle: Happy Number (Cycle Detection on a Number Sequence)

s1_definition.profdef: The happy number problem repeatedly transforms a number into the sum of the squares of its digits and asks whether this sequence reaches 1. Because the sequence either reaches 1 or falls into a repeating cycle, you can detect the cycle with Floyd's tortoise and hare on the generated values: a slow pointer advances one transformation per step and a fast pointer two, and if they meet at a value other than 1, the number is unhappy.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh runs a validation routine on an account code that keeps folding the code into a smaller number by squaring each digit and adding them up. If it eventually folds down to 1, the code is accepted as happy. If it never reaches 1, it must be going in circles forever. To spot the circle without remembering every number he has seen, he runs two folders, a slow one doing one fold per step and a fast one doing two, and if they ever land on the same number that is not 1, he knows the sequence loops and the code is unhappy.
s1_definition.oneliner: Fold digits into squared sums; reaching 1 is happy, meeting a repeat is a cycle, so use tortoise and hare.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The happy number problem repeatedly transforms a number into the sum of the squares of its digits and asks whether this sequence reaches 1. Because the sequence either reaches 1 or falls into a repeating cycle, you can detect the cycle with Floyd's tortoise and hare on the generated values: a slow pointer advances one transformation per step and a fast pointer two, and if they meet at a value other than 1, the number is unhappy.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh runs a validation routine on an account code that keeps folding the code into a smaller number by squaring each digit and adding them up. If it eventually folds down to 1, the code is accepted as happy. If it never reaches 1, it must be going in circles forever. To spot the circle without remembering every number he has seen, he runs two folders, a slow one doing one fold per step and a fast one doing two, and if they ever land on the same number that is not 1, he knows the sequence loops and the code is unhappy.

**One line to remember:** Fold digits into squared sums; reaching 1 is happy, meeting a repeat is a cycle, so use tortoise and hare.

sections.s2_technical:
The transformation takes a number, squares each of its digits, and sums those squares to produce the next number. For example 19 becomes 1 squared plus 9 squared, which is 1 plus 81, equal to 82. We keep applying this. A known mathematical fact is that this process either reaches 1, in which case the number is happy, or it enters a cycle that never includes 1, in which case the number is unhappy. There is no third possibility, because the values stay bounded and must eventually repeat.

Because the unhappy case is a cycle, this is really a cycle-detection problem in disguise, which is exactly what Floyd's tortoise and hare solves with constant extra space. We keep a slow value that applies the transformation once per step and a fast value that applies it twice per step. If the fast value reaches 1, the number is happy. If the slow and fast values ever become equal at some value other than 1, they have met inside a cycle, so the number is unhappy.

A finance usage example: consider the account code 19. The slow sequence is 19, 82, 68, and so on, while the fast sequence folds twice as fast. For 19 the sequence eventually reaches 1, so 19 is happy. For a number like 2, the sequence is 4, 16, 37, 58, 89, 145, 42, 20, 4, which cycles back to 4 without ever hitting 1, so 2 is unhappy, and the fast and slow pointers meet inside that cycle.

The senior-level nuance: the alternative is to store every value seen in a hash set and stop when a value repeats or 1 appears, which is simpler to write but uses extra space. Floyd's method uses constant space, which is the senior answer when space is emphasized. The transformation itself is computed by repeatedly taking the last digit with the modulo operation, squaring it, and stripping it off with integer division until the number is zero.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India uses a digit-folding checksum routine as one lightweight validation for certain legacy account codes. A code is considered valid if the folding process, which squares each digit and sums the squares, eventually reduces to 1. If it never reaches 1, it loops forever, and the validation must detect that loop rather than running indefinitely.

Problem 2 — The validation runs in a tight loop over many codes and must not allocate growing memory per code, so a constant-space cycle detection is preferred over remembering every intermediate value.

The code defines a `HappyCodeValidator` class with an `isHappy` method implementing the transformation and Floyd's cycle detection. A runnable demo validates a happy code and an unhappy code and logs the result.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the happy code 19 and the unhappy code 2.

Step 1: For 19, both slow and fast start at 19. In the first iteration slow folds once to 82, and fast folds twice: 19 to 82, then 82 to 68, so fast is 68. They are not equal.

Step 2: Slow folds to 68, and fast folds twice from 68 onward. The sequences continue, with fast always two folds ahead.

Step 3: The sequence for 19 is mathematically known to reach 1. At some iteration both slow and fast land on 1 simultaneously, the loop ends because slow equals fast, and since that common value is 1, the method reports 19 as happy.

Step 4: For 2, both start at 2. The folding sequence is 4, 16, 37, 58, 89, 145, 42, 20, 4, which cycles back to 4 and never touches 1.

Step 5: The slow and fast pointers meet inside this cycle at some value that is not 1. The loop ends with slow equal to fast but not equal to 1, so the method reports 2 as unhappy.

Final output:

```
Oct 27, 2026 6:55:00 PM com.bank.validation.HappyCodeDemo main
INFO: Code 19 is happy (valid).
INFO: 19 valid: true
WARNING: Code 2 is unhappy (cycles).
INFO: 2  valid: false
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Code 19:
    slow: 19 → 82 → 68 → ... → 1
    fast: 19 → 68 → ... → 1 (two folds per step)
    slow==fast==1 → HAPPY (valid)

  Code 2:
    sequence: 4→16→37→58→89→145→42→20→4 (cycle)
    slow,fast meet at value ≠ 1 → UNHAPPY (invalid)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The happy number problem defines a transformation that replaces a number with the sum of the squares of its digits and asks whether repeating this eventually reaches 1. The crucial mathematical fact is that this process has only two possible fates: it either reaches 1, making the number happy, or it falls into a repeating cycle that never contains 1, making it unhappy. Because the unhappy case is a cycle, this is fundamentally a cycle-detection problem.

That realization lets me solve it with Floyd's tortoise and hare using constant extra space. I keep a slow value that applies the digit-square transformation once per step and a fast value that applies it twice per step. If the fast value ever reaches 1, the number is happy. If the slow and fast values become equal at some value other than 1, they have met inside a cycle, so the number is unhappy. The transformation itself is straightforward: I peel off each digit with the modulo operator, square it, add it to a running sum, and strip the digit away with integer division until nothing remains.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this as a lightweight checksum validation for certain legacy account codes. A code was accepted only if the digit-folding process reduced it to 1, and if it never reached 1 it would loop forever, so the validator had to detect that loop rather than spinning indefinitely. Because the validation ran in a tight loop over many codes, I wanted constant memory per code, which is exactly what the two-pointer method provides.

The senior-level point I make is the connection to cycle detection and the space tradeoff. The simplest implementation stores every intermediate value in a hash set and stops when a value repeats or 1 appears, which is easy to write but uses extra memory proportional to the sequence length. Floyd's two-pointer method achieves the same result in constant space by exploiting the fact that the unhappy sequence is a cycle, and recognizing that a seemingly numeric puzzle is really the same loop-detection problem as a linked list is what shows the depth of understanding an interviewer is looking for.
